output:
Start the payment migration only after two things happen: the service owner signs the release ticket, and the operations lead confirms you can restore the rollback snapshot. Do not start the migration if either confirmation is missing. Before moving traffic, the release engineer must write down the start time, current error rate, and database replication delay.

In stage one, send 10% of traffic to the new service for 30 minutes. Keep an eye on payment failures, duplicate charges, p95 latency, and replication delay. A key rule: stop the migration right away if there is any duplicate charge. If payment failures stay above 0.5% for five minutes in a row, send 100% of traffic back to the old service. If p95 latency stays above 800 ms for ten minutes, pause and ask the service owner if you should keep going. These numbers are strict rules for decisions, not loose suggestions.

The team must keep watching these exact same numbers during the whole migration. Watching them matters because the team needs clear proof to make choices. Do not move forward just because the calendar or schedule says so. After a good 10% stage, switch to 50% traffic for 60 minutes and follow the exact same stop rules. Never jump straight to 100%, even if the first stage looks great.

Once you reach 100%, keep the old service ready to roll back for seven days. Save the migration log file at /var/log/payments/migration.json and add its checksum to ticket PAY-2048. You must run `payments verify --ticket PAY-2048` and have it pass before turning off the old service. Tell customer support before every traffic change, and do not delete old logs until the incident-review window ends.
